common_name: Superbells Lemon Slice Calibrachoa (Yellow and White Pinwheel Million Bells)

planting.note: Set out vegetatively propagated starts once nights stay reliably above freezing; this Proven Winners selection is prized for its two-tone yellow-and-white pinwheel pattern rather than a solid color.

directions: Lemon Slice stands apart from the solid-yellow Superbells and Callie selections already grown here through its bicolor bloom, each flower splitting into radiating wedges of soft yellow and white. Grow in fast-draining, slightly acidic potting mix and avoid letting the root zone sit wet, since calibrachoa roots are prone to rot in soggy media. A steady weekly feeding program keeps the pattern crisp and the cascading stems dense rather than sparse and stretched. No deadheading is needed, as spent blooms drop cleanly on their own through the season.
sources: Penn State Extension flower trial notes

common_name: Superbells Blackcurrant Punch Calibrachoa (Deep Purple-Black Two-Tone Million Bells)

planting.note: Transplant after frost danger passes; this Punch-series selection pairs a near-black throat with a lighter frilled edge, giving it a moodier palette than the brighter Pomegranate and Coralberry Punch selections.

directions: Blackcurrant Punch rounds out the Punch subseries with the darkest coloring of the group, its deep aubergine-black petals edged in a thin ruffled band of contrasting color. Because dark pigments can absorb more heat, give plants slightly more consistent moisture during peak summer to prevent flagging in hot afternoon sun. Feed weekly with a balanced, acid-forming fertilizer to keep the saturated color from fading, and rely on the plant's self-cleaning habit rather than manual deadheading. Works best massed in a basket or large pot where its dramatic color reads clearly against companion plants.
sources: University of Georgia Extension container gardening trials

common_name: Superbells Double Orange Calibrachoa (Fully Double Orange Million Bells)

planting.note: Plant rooted starts after last frost; the Superbells Double line produces fully doubled, ruffled blooms rather than the simple five-lobed flowers of standard Superbells and Callie selections already in this collection.

directions: Double Orange carries multiple layers of petals per bloom, giving it a fuller, almost rose-like appearance compared with the single-flowered Superbells Blue and Yellow already grown here. The extra petal count makes flowers slightly heavier, so consistent feeding and steady moisture help stems support the bloom load without collapsing. Grow in well-drained, slightly acidic media and avoid overhead watering late in the day, since dense doubled flowers can hold moisture and become prone to botrytis in humid weather. No pinching is required, though a light trim in midsummer refreshes a leggy plant.
sources: Michigan State University Extension floriculture notes

common_name: Superbells Double Smitten Pink Calibrachoa (Fully Double Bright Fuchsia Million Bells)

planting.note: Set out after frost danger has passed; Double Smitten Pink brings a saturated, bright fuchsia to the doubled Superbells line, distinct from the softer rose of Callie Rose already represented here.

directions: Double Smitten Pink packs many small petals into each bloom, producing a denser, more textured flower than the single, saucer-shaped forms typical of most calibrachoa. Keep the growing medium evenly moist but never waterlogged, since the doubled flower form is more prone to fungal spotting when petals stay wet overhead. Regular weekly feeding sustains the vivid pink through the hottest part of summer, and the trailing stems benefit from a light shear if growth becomes thin at the base. Pair with cooler-toned companions to let the saturated pink stand out in a mixed container.
sources: Oregon State University Extension annual flower trials

common_name: Cabaret Bright Red Calibrachoa (Vigorous Trailing Scarlet Million Bells)

planting.note: Plant vegetatively propagated liners after hard frost risk ends; Cabaret is a Ball FloraPlant/Selecta One series bred for pot-tight production, needing little to no pinching or growth regulator to stay full.

directions: Cabaret Bright Red brings a clear, saturated scarlet to the genus, distinguishing itself from the darker ruby tone of Callie Dark Red already in this dataset. The series is bred for medium vigor and early flowering, so young plants fill a hanging basket or 4- to 6-inch pot quickly without heavy pinching. Provide fast-draining, slightly acidic soil and steady but not excessive moisture, since calibrachoa roots decline quickly in saturated media. Weekly liquid feeding keeps the trailing stems dense and the color from washing out under intense summer sun.

common_name: Cabaret Deep Blue Calibrachoa (Vigorous Trailing Violet-Blue Million Bells)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings after frost danger passes; Cabaret Deep Blue carries a richer, more saturated violet-blue than the lighter Superbells Blue already grown here.

directions: Deep Blue's dense, mounding-to-trailing habit fills containers quickly thanks to the Cabaret series' medium vigor, making it well suited to smaller pots that would be overwhelmed by larger trailing calibrachoa. Grow in well-drained, slightly acidic potting mix and avoid letting the medium dry out completely between waterings, as drought stress causes rapid flower drop. Weekly fertilization keeps the deep violet-blue color intense rather than fading toward a washed-out lavender. The plant self-cleans continuously, so spent flowers require no manual removal.

common_name: Kabloom Cherry Calibrachoa (Seed-Grown Trailing Cherry-Red Million Bells)

planting.note: Start indoors 10-12 weeks before the last frost or purchase started plugs, since Kabloom is the first calibrachoa series bred to grow true from seed rather than propagate only from cuttings.

directions: Kabloom Cherry is notable mainly for its production method: unlike the vegetatively propagated Superbells, Callie, and MiniFamous selections already in this dataset, it is a true seed strain, giving growers a lower-cost path to a compact, self-branching plant covered in bright cherry-red blooms. Seedlings are slower to establish than rooted cuttings, so keep young plants under consistent warmth and moisture until roots fill the cell. Once established, the plant tolerates heat and drought better than many vegetative calibrachoa, though it still performs best with regular weekly feeding. No deadheading is required, as the self-cleaning flowers drop cleanly.

common_name: Kabloom Deep Pink Calibrachoa (Seed-Grown Trailing Deep Pink Million Bells)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 10-12 weeks before the last frost or buy started plugs; Kabloom Deep Pink gives growers a seed-propagated alternative to cutting-grown pink calibrachoa such as Callie Rose already in this dataset.

directions: Deep Pink offers a richer, more saturated pink than the softer rose tones typical of vegetative calibrachoa lines, and being a true seed strain it germinates and branches uniformly across a flat, simplifying large-scale production. Provide bottom heat during germination and keep the seed-starting mix evenly moist but not saturated, since calibrachoa seed is fine and easily displaced or rotted by heavy watering. After transplanting, the compact, self-branching habit needs minimal pinching to fill out a basket or container. Weekly feeding and full sun keep the deep pink color vibrant through the heat of summer.

common_name: Can-Can Apricot Calibrachoa (Semi-Double Peach and Rose-Pink Million Bells)

planting.note: Plant vegetatively propagated starts after frost danger passes; Can-Can Apricot (bred as 'Balcanapt') produces semi-double, ruffled flowers rather than the flat single form of most calibrachoa in this collection.

directions: Can-Can Apricot's semi-double blooms open peach at the center and shade toward rose-pink at the ruffled petal edges, giving each flower a two-tone frilled look distinct from the smooth single trumpets of Superbells and Callie selections already grown here. The extra petal layers add slight weight to each bloom, so keep the plant well fed and avoid letting the potting mix dry to the point of wilting, which stresses the doubled flower form more than single-flowered types. Use fast-draining, slightly acidic media and full sun for best flower coverage. The trailing stems benefit from an occasional light trim to encourage fresh branching if the center of the plant becomes bare.
